talks.title: What is ATT&CK Coverage, Anyway? | Adam Mashinchi | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Reviews what is ATT&CK Coverage, Anyway? | Adam Mashinchi | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Adam Mashinchi presents at Wild West Hackin' Fest on ATT&CK coverage, completing a trilogy of talks exploring what coverage means and how organizations measure defensive effectiveness.

Key Topics: Defining ATT&CK coverage beyond checkbox compliance; building coverage measurement programs; prior talks at Wild West Hackin' Fest and ATT&CKcon; and practical guidance for spinning up coverage initiatives.

Technical Details: Mashinchi wraps up a three-talk series on ATT&CK coverage, providing updated guidance on measuring which techniques organizations can detect and respond to, moving beyond simply mapping controls to the framework.

Takeaways: ATT&CK coverage requires meaningful measurement of detection and response capability, not just control mapping. Organizations should build programs that validate actual defensive effectiveness.

talks.title: Data is the New Oil | Jeremiah Fowler | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Analyzes data is the New Oil | Jeremiah Fowler | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
From Breach to Research Career

Jeremiah Fowler describes himself as a data hunter, not a deep technical wizard. He entered security after a company data breach while he served as communications and PR director, learning data protection the hard way and later building an internal research center and hiring the researcher who reported the flaw.

Personal Path and Ukraine

His talk weaves career pivots—from Myspace glitter text and a failed music career through subprime-era finance—to moving to Kyiv with his Ukrainian partner. After Russia's invasion, he recounts a four-day wait at the Polish border with his daughter, reflecting on passport privilege amid refugee hardship.

Data as Valuable Asset

Fowler frames exposed data as today's oil: widely sought and routinely mishandled. He cites statistics that nearly 60% of businesses suffered a breach in three years, and argues firms typically invest in security only after an incident—joking that nobody runs a bug bounty until they need one.

Discovery Work in Practice

His Security Discovery work treats open-data hunting as investigative treasure seeking. Examples include railway-station Wi-Fi providers exposing visitor data. The session emphasizes how breach-driven awareness, researcher partnerships, and proactive data exposure hunting can shift organizational priorities.

talks.title: Making the Case for SCA | Alyssa Miller | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Outlines making the Case for SCA | Alyssa Miller | WWHF San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
From Monoliths to Dependency Trees

Alyssa Miller, business information security officer and former developer, contrasts pre-2004 applications written entirely in-house with modern builds pulling transitive dependencies through Maven, npm, and similar package managers. Developers often cannot enumerate indirect libraries buried deep in dependency graphs.

Landmark Supply-Chain Breaches

Miller revisits Equifax's 2017 breach via an unpatched Apache Struts dependency nested below visible manifests, exposing 164 million consumers. She connects the pattern to Log4j in late 2021—present in 91% of Java apps per Snyk, often as unknown indirect dependencies—and Spring4Shell in 2022, showing the problem accelerating rather than resolved.

The Aviation Weight-and-Balance Analogy

Drawing on her pilot training, Miller compares software composition analysis to aircraft equipment manifests that track every component's weight and position for safe flight. Organizations need analogous visibility into third-party code affecting application center of gravity and risk.

Making the Case for SCA

The talk argues software composition analysis tools, accurate inventories, and developer integration are essential defenses. Without knowing what ships inside binaries, organizations cannot patch, prioritize, or insure against vulnerabilities in code they never wrote but implicitly trust.

talks.title: Securing Down Ballot Political Campaigns: The Next Frontier | Daniel Bardenstein | San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Analyzes securing Down Ballot Political Campaigns: The Next Frontier | Daniel Bardenstein | San Diego 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Down-ballot threat model

Daniel Bardenstein argues election security discourse focuses on presidential races while state and local campaigns face serious but under-resourced threats. Even small challenger campaigns hold data and infrastructure attackers can disrupt, and every seat affects national governance.

Campaign security gaps

Volunteering for a friend’s congressional primary, he found egregious practices uncommon in enterprise environments: questionable web hosting, limited backend access for defensive scripts, and no budget for professional security tooling. Campaign staff often prioritize fundraising over infrastructure hardening.

DDoS and attribution limits

After DDoS attacks traced to EC2 infrastructure, reporting to authorities yielded little response. Forensics and hardening helped, but the candidate ultimately lost the primary. Bardenstein uses the case to highlight that private citizens and volunteer teams cannot match nation-state or organized troll capabilities alone.
